scope: Kubernetes GPU device resources, probes, Deployment rollout, PDB and vLLM Production Stack.

claims.claim: Kubernetes exposes vendor GPU resources through device plugins; NVIDIA nodes commonly advertise nvidia.com/gpu after drivers and the NVIDIA device plugin are installed.
claims.notes: MIG and GPU-sharing plugins can expose different resource names and allocation semantics.

claims.claim: Kubernetes GPU resources are specified in limits; limits may be used as requests when requests are omitted, requests and limits must match when both are set, and GPU requests without limits are not allowed.
claims.notes: This applies to the extended GPU resources documented by Kubernetes; plugin-specific sharing schemes can differ.

claims.claim: Startup probes delay liveness and readiness probes until initialization succeeds; readiness removes non-ready Pods from Service traffic; liveness failure can restart the container.
claims.notes: The example thresholds in the chapter are illustrative and must be tuned for model load time.

claims.claim: Kubernetes Deployment RollingUpdate uses maxUnavailable and maxSurge to control unavailable and additional Pods during rollout.
claims.notes: GPU scheduling capacity can prevent surge Pods from starting even when rollout settings permit them.

claims.claim: PodDisruptionBudget limits simultaneous voluntary disruptions; it does not prevent involuntary node failures and does not replace Deployment rolling update strategy.
claims.notes: PDB semantics differ from Deployment rollout controls.

claims.claim: Current vLLM Production Stack documentation lists Helm Chart, CRD and Gateway API Inference Extension as three primary deployment options.
claims.notes: Each mode has its own version and component compatibility requirements.

claims.claim: Production Stack load-aware routing scores an endpoint using matched prompt tokens divided by prompt tokens minus beta times relative endpoint load.
claims.notes: This is one router implementation, not a universal routing algorithm.
